title: U.S. Military's Cold War-Era M14 Rifles to Be Sold to Public for First Time
excerpt: The Civilian Marksmanship Program will convert over 100,000 surplus M14 rifles to semi-automatic and offer them to qualified citizens beginning late 2026.
body:
• The Civilian Marksmanship Program has received special authorization to sell surplus M14 rifles after converting them to permanent semi-automatic configuration
  • Senator Cynthia Lummis said 100,000 M14s will be made available, with first orders expected in late 2026 or early 2027
  • The sale marks a major shift in ATF policy, which previously held that any receiver built as a machine gun could never be reclassified
  • Prices are expected to range from $4,000 to $6,000, with proceeds funding marksmanship training and youth programs

The Civilian Marksmanship Program has announced it will begin selling surplus U.S. military M14 rifles to qualified American citizens — the first time these iconic Cold War-era service rifles will reach the civilian market in their original military form.

The rifles, which served as the U.S. Army's standard-issue weapon beginning in 1957, will be permanently and irreversibly converted to semi-automatic operation before sale. The CMP anticipates fulfilling first orders in late 2026 or early 2027, though pricing, purchase limits, and ordering procedures have not yet been finalized.

A Historic Shift in Firearms Policy

The announcement represents a significant departure from longstanding Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives policy. The ATF has traditionally maintained that any firearm receiver originally manufactured as a machine gun retains that classification permanently, regardless of later modifications. Because all military M14s were built as select-fire rifles, most firearms enthusiasts assumed they would never be legally sold to civilians.

https://x.com/starsandstripes/status/2087315373708157143

The CMP's special authorization appears to carve out an exception for this specific class of surplus military rifles. Whether the decision will have broader implications for other surplus firearms remains unclear.

U.S. Senator Cynthia Lummis of Wyoming announced that 100,000 M14 rifles would be made available through the program. "Proceeds will fund marksmanship training and youth programs nationwide, including at the new Wyoming State Shooting Complex in Cody, which will partner with CMP," Lummis said.

The M14's Military Legacy

Designed by John C. Garand as the direct descendant of the legendary M1 Garand, the M14 was chambered in the new 7.62x51mm NATO cartridge and featured a detachable box magazine. It was intended to replace not just the M1 rifle but also the M1 and M2 Carbines, the M3A1 submachine gun, and the Browning Automatic Rifle.

The rifle's tenure as America's primary service weapon was relatively brief. By the mid-1960s, the Pentagon began fielding Eugene Stoner's AR-15 platform as the M16 for the Vietnam War, and M14 production ended in 1965. Modified variants continued in service as designated marksman and sniper rifles into the late 1980s, and the weapon still sees limited ceremonial use today.

"By special authorization, the CMP is pleased to announce the future availability and sale of surplus M14 rifles. Prior to sale, the rifles will be modified to be permanently and irreversibly semi-automatic rifles."

— Civilian Marksmanship Program official announcement

Only 1.38 million M14s were manufactured by Springfield Armory, Harrington & Richardson, TRW, and Winchester between 1959 and 1965 — a fraction of the more than 5 million M1 Garands produced. Of those, approximately 479,000 were destroyed at Anniston Army Depot during the Clinton administration, and another 321,000 were distributed as military aid to countries including South Vietnam, Estonia, Turkey, Greece, the Philippines, and Ukraine.

What Buyers Can Expect

Specific pricing has not been released, but industry speculation puts estimates between $4,000 and $6,000 per rifle. The CMP, a federally chartered nonprofit, will sell the rifles through both mail order and its physical stores. Buyers must meet standard CMP eligibility requirements, which include proof of U.S. citizenship, membership in a CMP-affiliated organization, and a background check.

The sale has generated enormous interest in the firearms community. While commercial semi-automatic reproductions like the Springfield Armory M1A have been available for decades, the opportunity to own a genuine military-issue M14 with documented service history is unprecedented.

Looking Ahead

The CMP has not yet published details on the semi-automatic conversion process, purchase limits per buyer, or specific grading and pricing tiers. The organization said additional information would be released at a later date. Proceeds from all CMP sales fund firearms safety education, marksmanship competitions, scholarships, and youth programs nationwide.
